title: “Then, while the Venerable Udāyi was in solitary retreat, this thought arose in his mind: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned many painful states for…
content: “Then, while the Venerable Udāyi was in solitary retreat, this thought arose in his mind: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned many painful states for us. Indeed, the Blessed One has brought us many pleasant states. Indeed, the Blessed One has abandoned many unwholesome states for us. Indeed, the Blessed One has brought us many wholesome states.’”

title: Venerable Ajita: “By what is the world shrouded? Why does it not shine forth? What do you call its defilement? What is its great fear?”…
content:
Venerable Ajita:
“By what is the world shrouded?
Why does it not shine forth?
What do you call its defilement?
What is its great fear?”

The Blessed One:
“The world is shrouded by ignorance.
Through stinginess and heedlessness it does not shine forth.
I say longing is its defilement —
Suffering is its great fear.”

title: “If there were no gratification in form, monks, beings would not become lustful for form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become lustful…
content: “If there were no gratification in form, monks, beings would not become lustful for form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become lustful for form. If there were no peril in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because there is peril in form, beings become disenchanted with form. If there were no escape from form, beings would not escape from form. But because there is escape from form, beings escape from form. Monks, as long as beings do not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in regard to these six internal sense bases, they have not, monks, along with this world of devas, Māras, Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, dwelt with minds free from clinging, detached, liberated, unbounded. But because beings have directly known them as they actually are, therefore they have dwelt with minds free from clinging, detached, liberated, unbounded.”

title: “Monks, how is it that Māra and his followers cannot reach? Here, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states,…
content: “Monks, how is it that Māra and his followers cannot reach? Here, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, obliterated Māra’s track, leaving no trace, making Māra unable to find his path. Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, without initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called a monk who has blinded Māra, obliterated Māra’s track, leaving no trace, making Māra unable to find his path.”

title: “Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove to a person who had just died. Monks, when he saw the corpse of a dead person, Prince…
content: “Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove to a person who had just died. Monks, when he saw the corpse of a dead person, Prince Vipassī asked: ‘Good man, why is this person called dead?’ ‘Your Highness, he is called dead because now his mother, father, and other blood relatives no longer see him; and he no longer sees his mother, father, or other blood relatives.’ ‘Good man, then am I not dead — will I be subject to death? Will my father, mother, or other blood relatives not see me? And will I not see my father, mother, or other blood relatives?’ ‘Your Highness, you and I as well — even though we are not yet dead, we will die. Your father, mother, and other blood relatives will not see you, and you will not see your father, mother, or other blood relatives.’ ‘Good man, then this visit to the pleasure garden is enough. Drive back to the palace.’ ‘Yes, Your Highness.’ Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove back to the palace. Monks, Prince Vipassī returned to the palace, suffering, grieving, and thought: ‘Shameful indeed is this birth! And anyone who is born must age, must be sick, must die like this!’”

title: The hunter set his trap and snare, The wise deer does not approach, Having eaten the crops, we go our way, Leaving the trapper to…
content:
The hunter set his trap and snare,
The wise deer does not approach,
Having eaten the crops, we go our way,
Leaving the trapper to lament.

title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that so gives rise to unarisen sensual desire, or to the increase and expansion of arisen sensual…
content: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that so gives rise to unarisen sensual desire, or to the increase and expansion of arisen sensual desire, as the sign of the beautiful. The sign of the beautiful, monks, when unwisely attended to, gives rise to unarisen sensual desire and increases and expands arisen sensual desire.”

title: "Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the…
content: "Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the mind faculty, practices the restraint of the mind faculty. By means of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences an internal feeling of ease, unblemished."

title: “Monks, what are the further things that should be done? ‘We must guard the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, do not grasp…
content: “Monks, what are the further things that should be done? ‘We must guard the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—we will restrain that cause, guard the eye, practice restraint of the eye. When the ear hears a sound … nose smells an odor … tongue tastes a flavor … body feels a touch … mind cognizes phenomena, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—we will restrain that cause, guard the mind, practice restraint of the mind.’”

title: “Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Whatever sensual pleasures present and future, whatever perceptions of sensual pleasure present and future, whatever forms present and future…
content: “Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Whatever sensual pleasures present and future, whatever perceptions of sensual pleasure present and future, whatever forms present and future — all are the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements.’ While he practices thus, dwells often thus, his mind becomes serene in that element. With serene mind, he attains the Imperturbable (āneñja) either in this very life or he becomes strongly inclined to wisdom. At the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness, proceeding accordingly, may attain the Imperturbable.”
